question: What is the difference between overfitting and generalisation in supervised learning?
answer: Generalisation is the ability of a model to perform well on new, unseen data. Overfitting occurs when a model learns the training data too closely, which results in it failing to perform well on new examples.
ground_truth: Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data too closely and performs poorly on new unseen data. Generalisation refers to a model performing well on data it was not trained on, which is the actual goal of supervised learning.

chunks.text: Supervised learning is a type of machine learning where a model is trained on labelled data. Each training example has an input and a known correct output. The model learns to map inputs to outputs by minimising a loss function over many examples. Common algorithms include linear regression for continuous outputs and logistic regression for classification. The key challenge is generalisation — the model must perform well on data it has never seen, not just on the training set. Overfitting occurs when the model learns the training data too closely and fails on new examples. Techniques like cross-validation, regularisation, and dropout help prevent this.
chunks.title: Supervised Learning

chunks.text: A neural network is a function approximator made up of layers of nodes called neurons. Each neuron takes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias, and passes the result through an activation function such as ReLU or sigmoid. The network learns by adjusting weights using backpropagation — an algorithm that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight using the chain rule. Stochastic gradient descent then updates the weights in the direction that reduces the loss. Deeper networks can learn more complex representations but require more data and are harder to train. Batch normalisation and skip connections were introduced to address these training difficulties.
chunks.title: Neural Networks

chunks.text: Large language models are transformer-based models trained on massive text corpora to predict the next token in a sequence. Scale has proven to be the primary driver of capability — models with more parameters trained on more data consistently outperform smaller ones on a wide range of tasks. GPT-4, LLaMA, and Gemini are examples of modern LLMs. These models are typically fine-tuned after pretraining using reinforcement learning from human feedback to align their outputs with human preferences. A known limitation is hallucination — LLMs sometimes generate confident-sounding but factually incorrect statements because they model token distributions rather than ground truth.

answer: Backpropagation trains a neural network by computing the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight using the chain rule, which allows stochastic gradient descent to update the weights in the direction that reduces the loss.
ground_truth: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight using the chain rule, then stochastic gradient descent updates the weights in the direction that reduces the loss.

chunks.text: The transformer architecture, introduced by Vaswani et al. in 2017, replaced recurrent networks for sequence modelling tasks. Its core mechanism is self-attention, which allows every position in a sequence to directly attend to every other position. This removes the sequential bottleneck of RNNs and enables parallelisation during training. The encoder maps an input sequence to a set of continuous representations, and the decoder generates the output sequence one token at a time. Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings to give the model information about token order, since self-attention itself is permutation-invariant.

chunks.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, introduced by Lewis et al. in 2020, addresses the hallucination problem of LLMs by grounding answers in retrieved documents. At query time, the system retrieves the most relevant passages from an external knowledge base and passes them alongside the question to the LLM. The model is instructed to answer only from the provided context. This approach allows the knowledge base to be updated without retraining the model and provides traceable citations for each answer. The quality of a RAG system depends heavily on retrieval quality — if the wrong documents are retrieved, the LLM cannot produce a correct answer regardless of its capability.
chunks.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation

chunks.text: Evaluating RAG systems is more complex than evaluating a standard classifier because quality depends on two separate components: the retriever and the generator. The RAGAS framework defines four core metrics. Faithfulness measures whether each claim in the generated answer is supported by the retrieved context. Answer relevancy measures how directly the answer addresses the question. Context precision measures the proportion of retrieved chunks that are actually relevant to the question. Context recall measures whether all the information needed to answer the question was present in the retrieved chunks. Taken together, these metrics give a diagnostic view of where a pipeline is failing.
chunks.title: RAG Evaluation

chunks.text: Fine-tuning modifies the weights of a pretrained model on a task-specific dataset. It is effective for teaching the model a new style, format, or domain-specific terminology. However, it is expensive to repeat when knowledge changes, and the model can still hallucinate on facts it learned during fine-tuning. RAG keeps the base model frozen and instead supplies relevant context at inference time. This makes knowledge updates cheap — you only need to update the document store. For factual question answering over changing data, RAG is generally preferred. For tasks where the model needs to change its behaviour or output format, fine-tuning is more appropriate. The two approaches can also be combined.

question: What makes two text embeddings similar to each other?
answer: Based on the context, two text embeddings are similar (close to each other in vector space) if they represent sentences with similar semantic meanings, even if those sentences share no words.
ground_truth: Two embeddings are similar when the texts they represent have similar meanings. Semantic similarity is captured as closeness in vector space, measured by cosine similarity or dot product.

chunks.text: Vector embeddings are dense numerical representations of text that capture semantic meaning. Two sentences with similar meanings will have embeddings that are close to each other in vector space, even if they share no words. Embeddings are produced by encoder models trained on large corpora. In RAG systems, both the documents in the knowledge base and the user query are embedded, and retrieval is performed by finding the documents whose embeddings are closest to the query embedding. Cosine similarity and dot product are the most common distance metrics used. The quality of the embedding model directly affects retrieval quality and therefore the overall RAG pipeline performance.
chunks.title: Vector Embeddings

chunks.text: Chunking is the process of splitting documents into smaller pieces before embedding them. It matters because embedding an entire document produces a vector that represents the average meaning of the whole document, which is too broad to match a specific query accurately. Smaller chunks are more precise but may lack context. A common approach is to use fixed-size chunks of around 300 to 500 tokens with an overlap of 10 to 20 percent between consecutive chunks. The overlap ensures that information at chunk boundaries is not lost. Sentence-level chunking and semantic chunking are alternatives that try to split at natural content boundaries rather than fixed token counts.
chunks.title: Chunking Strategy

chunks.text: Vector databases are purpose-built storage systems for high-dimensional embeddings. Unlike relational databases that search by exact match, vector databases support approximate nearest-neighbour search, which finds the most similar embeddings to a query vector efficiently at scale. ChromaDB, Pinecone, Weaviate, and Qdrant are widely used options. ChromaDB is popular for local development and research because it runs in-process with no external service required. Pinecone is a managed cloud service used in production systems. The choice of vector database affects query latency, scalability, and cost but does not affect the quality of the embeddings themselves.
chunks.title: Vector Databases

question: What is faithfulness as a RAG evaluation metric?
answer: Faithfulness measures whether each claim in the generated answer is supported by the retrieved context.
ground_truth: Faithfulness measures whether each claim in the generated answer is supported by the retrieved context rather than being made up by the model.

chunks.text: Evaluating RAG systems is more complex than evaluating a standard classifier because quality depends on two separate components: the retriever and the generator. The RAGAS framework defines four core metrics. Faithfulness measures whether each claim in the generated answer is supported by the retrieved context. Answer relevancy measures how directly the answer addresses the question. Context precision measures the proportion of retrieved chunks that are actually relevant to the question. Context recall measures whether all the information needed to answer the question was present in the retrieved chunks. Taken together, these metrics give a diagnostic view of where a pipeline is failing.
chunks.title: RAG Evaluation

chunks.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, introduced by Lewis et al. in 2020, addresses the hallucination problem of LLMs by grounding answers in retrieved documents. At query time, the system retrieves the most relevant passages from an external knowledge base and passes them alongside the question to the LLM. The model is instructed to answer only from the provided context. This approach allows the knowledge base to be updated without retraining the model and provides traceable citations for each answer. The quality of a RAG system depends heavily on retrieval quality — if the wrong documents are retrieved, the LLM cannot produce a correct answer regardless of its capability.
chunks.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation

chunks.text: Vector embeddings are dense numerical representations of text that capture semantic meaning. Two sentences with similar meanings will have embeddings that are close to each other in vector space, even if they share no words. Embeddings are produced by encoder models trained on large corpora. In RAG systems, both the documents in the knowledge base and the user query are embedded, and retrieval is performed by finding the documents whose embeddings are closest to the query embedding. Cosine similarity and dot product are the most common distance metrics used. The quality of the embedding model directly affects retrieval quality and therefore the overall RAG pipeline performance.
chunks.title: Vector Embeddings

question: What is the role of the encoder in a transformer model?
answer: The encoder maps an input sequence to a set of continuous representations.
ground_truth: The encoder maps an input sequence to a set of continuous representations that capture the meaning of the input.

chunks.text: The transformer architecture, introduced by Vaswani et al. in 2017, replaced recurrent networks for sequence modelling tasks. Its core mechanism is self-attention, which allows every position in a sequence to directly attend to every other position. This removes the sequential bottleneck of RNNs and enables parallelisation during training. The encoder maps an input sequence to a set of continuous representations, and the decoder generates the output sequence one token at a time. Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings to give the model information about token order, since self-attention itself is permutation-invariant.

chunks.text: Large language models are transformer-based models trained on massive text corpora to predict the next token in a sequence. Scale has proven to be the primary driver of capability — models with more parameters trained on more data consistently outperform smaller ones on a wide range of tasks. GPT-4, LLaMA, and Gemini are examples of modern LLMs. These models are typically fine-tuned after pretraining using reinforcement learning from human feedback to align their outputs with human preferences. A known limitation is hallucination — LLMs sometimes generate confident-sounding but factually incorrect statements because they model token distributions rather than ground truth.
chunks.title: Large Language Models

question: Why is RAG preferred over fine-tuning for factual question answering over changing data?
answer: RAG is preferred for factual question answering over changing data because it keeps the base model frozen and supplies relevant context at inference time, making knowledge updates cheap by requiring only an update to the document store.
ground_truth: With RAG, updating knowledge only requires updating the document store. Fine-tuning would require retraining the model each time the knowledge changes, which is expensive.

chunks.text: Fine-tuning modifies the weights of a pretrained model on a task-specific dataset. It is effective for teaching the model a new style, format, or domain-specific terminology. However, it is expensive to repeat when knowledge changes, and the model can still hallucinate on facts it learned during fine-tuning. RAG keeps the base model frozen and instead supplies relevant context at inference time. This makes knowledge updates cheap — you only need to update the document store. For factual question answering over changing data, RAG is generally preferred. For tasks where the model needs to change its behaviour or output format, fine-tuning is more appropriate. The two approaches can also be combined.
chunks.title: Fine-Tuning vs RAG

chunks.text: Vector databases are purpose-built storage systems for high-dimensional embeddings. Unlike relational databases that search by exact match, vector databases support approximate nearest-neighbour search, which finds the most similar embeddings to a query vector efficiently at scale. ChromaDB, Pinecone, Weaviate, and Qdrant are widely used options. ChromaDB is popular for local development and research because it runs in-process with no external service required. Pinecone is a managed cloud service used in production systems. The choice of vector database affects query latency, scalability, and cost but does not affect the quality of the embeddings themselves.
chunks.title: Vector Databases

question: What activation functions are used in neural networks?
answer: ReLU and sigmoid.
ground_truth: Common activation functions include ReLU and sigmoid.

chunks.text: A neural network is a function approximator made up of layers of nodes called neurons. Each neuron takes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias, and passes the result through an activation function such as ReLU or sigmoid. The network learns by adjusting weights using backpropagation — an algorithm that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight using the chain rule. Stochastic gradient descent then updates the weights in the direction that reduces the loss. Deeper networks can learn more complex representations but require more data and are harder to train. Batch normalisation and skip connections were introduced to address these training difficulties.

question: What does answer relevancy measure in RAG evaluation?
answer: Answer relevancy measures how directly the generated answer addresses the question.
ground_truth: Answer relevancy measures how directly and completely the generated answer addresses the question that was asked.
